As of 306 AM EDT Tuesday...

KEY MESSAGE 1: Following an active evening of showers and 
thunderstorms, especially in northern portions of our region, today 
will be a reprieve with only modest wind gusts on the backside of 
departing low pressure. Northwesterly breezes will be somewhat 
refreshing with somewhat drier air being advected in from a heavily 
modified polar air mass, with some of the deeper mixing supporting a 
few gusts to around 25 MPH, although 850 millibar winds will 
decrease through the afternoon hours, limiting the magnitude of 
gusts despite steepening low level lapse rates. Meager instability 
and anti-cyclonic flow will yield near zero PoPs for our entire 
region. 

By Wednesday afternoon, it appears some variety of trough will swing 
in from the northwest, and with a subtle surface trough out ahead of 
it in southern Canada, isolated showers will develop with greatest 
chances in northern New York. Instability downstream in our area 
looks fairly low (under 1000 J/kg), driven by steep low level lapse 
rates, while humidity near the surface and aloft remains muted 
compared to recent days along with poor mid-level lapse rates. 
Therefore, the threat of either heavy rainfall or severe weather is 
not evident at this time with any of the showers that develop, and 
with greater instability to our north, the greatest threat of 
locally strong thunderstorm wind gusts will be towards the 
International Border as thunderstorms track towards the southeast 
late in the day. The timing in the latest convection allowing models 
(CAMs) for any heavier variety of showers generally looks after 2 
PM, with highest probabilities between around 5 and 8 PM. The swath 
for these showers currently is favored for northern New York and 
somewhat less likely in northern Vermont, with again little or no 
chance of rain in southern portions of Vermont. Overnight Wednesday 
the convective chances are a little more unclear, dependent on how 
widespread and intense any of the storms in southern Canada earlier 
in the day wind up being. Remnants of those storms would provide us 
with precipitation potentially Wednesday night, with otherwise quiet 
weather. 

Temperatures through the next couple of days will remain rather 
seasonable with minimal change in 850 millibar temperatures, which 
look near the climatological normals, supporting highs each day in 
the mid 70s to low 80s and lows in the 50s for most locations.

KEY MESSAGE 2: A seasonably potent low pressure system will pass near 
or north of the region later Thursday into Friday. Widespread rain 
can be expected with this system, with convective weather more 
uncertain and relatively limited compared to recent events. Model 
consensus on the timing/track of the primary shortwave supports a 
cold frontal passage Thursday night. Generally the ingredients don't 
look particularly favorable for heavy rainfall ahead of the front, 
given the dominance of polar influence in the mid and upper air flow 
and westerly rather than southerly near surface winds, limiting deep 
moisture with lack of warm rain processes. With regards to severe 
weather, seasonably warm air and height falls still will support 
some CAPE, presenting a low CAPE, high shear scenario that will need 
to be monitored for low-topped convection, particularly in the 
vicinity of the system's warm front or effective warm front. The 
latest blend of models shows a swath of moderate rainfall (0.5" to 
1") roughly from Franklin County, New York eastward to Franklin 
County, Vermont, with lesser amounts trending southward, which seems 
reasonable given global ensemble support for heavy rainfall is non-
existent (probabilities of rainfall exceeding 1" are under 5% in 24 
hours).

KEY MESSAGE 3: Models continue to favor the closing off of low pressure 
east of Vermont Friday. This will support a Northwest flow pattern 
likely resulting in a few upslope rain showers as maritime air wraps 
around the low. Heating in the afternoon could result in the 
triggering of a few thunderstorms. 

Over the weekend, much drier air moves into the region as high 
pressure pushes the low along the longwave pattern. Conditions will 
likely be quite pleasant Saturday with dewpoints in the 40s and 50s 
with temperatures generally in the 70s. The ridge axis is projected 
to shift eastward Sunday and supports warmer highs for broad valleys 
to around 80 degrees while dew points dry further remaining more in 
the 40s. Overall, these conditions are shaping up to be near ideal 
weather for outdoor activities. The next wave that will bring 
precipitation to the Northeast will be early next week as zonal flow 
keeps the pattern progressive. Temperatures should warm a degree or 
Monday and Tuesday as low level flow turns southwesterly.
